facts.statement: Moabosaurus is a genus of turiasaurian sauropod dinosaur found in the Early Cretaceous Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah, United States.
facts.quote: Moabosaurus (meaning "Moab reptile") is a genus of turiasaurian sauropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah, United States.

facts.statement: Fossils of Moabosaurus were collected from the Dalton Wells Quarry, located about 20 km northwest of Moab, Utah.
facts.quote: Moabosaurus was collected from the Dalton Wells Quarry, which is about 20 km northwest of Moab, Utah.

facts.statement: Between 1975 and 2005, the Dalton Wells Quarry yielded parts of at least 18 individuals of Moabosaurus, totaling over 5,500 bones.
facts.quote: Between 1975 and 2005, the quarry produced parts of at least 18 individuals of Moabosaurus based on the number of braincases present, totalling over 5,500 bones.

facts.statement: Many Moabosaurus bones are fragmentary due to intense trampling, evidenced by breakage and scratches.
facts.quote: Many of the recovered bones are fragmentary due to intense trampling as evidenced by breakage and trample scratches.

facts.statement: Evidence of burrows and mandible marks suggests that beetle larvae consumed portions of Moabosaurus bones before burial.
facts.quote: Insects, probably beetle larvae, consumed portions of the bones that were in contact with the ground, as evidenced by burrows and mandible marks.

facts.statement: Moabosaurus utahensis was named by Brooks B. Britt, Rodney D. Scheets, Michael F. Whiting, and D. Ray Wilhite.
facts.quote: Brooks B. Britt, Rodney D. Scheets, Michael F. Whiting, and D. Ray Wilhite named Moabosaurus utahensis.

facts.statement: Detrital zircon crystals date the Dalton Wells Quarry to 125 million years ago, indicating Moabosaurus lived during the Aptian age.
facts.quote: Detrital zircon crystals from the Dalton Wells Quarry yield an age of 125 million years, indicating Moabosaurus is Aptian in age.

facts.statement: Moabosaurus is characterized by thin, low neural spines, transverse ridges in specific vertebrae, strongly procoelous caudal vertebrae, and an ulna with well-developed ridges and a large olecranon process.
facts.quote: Moabosaurus is characterized by a suite of features including: extremely low neural spines that are thin, transverse ridges in the posterior cervical vertebrae and anterior dorsal vertebrae; strongly procoelous proximal and distal caudal vertebrae; and an ulna with well-developed lateral and medial anteroproximal ridges combined with a large olecranon process.

facts.statement: While the 2017 description estimated Moabosaurus reached 10 meters (32.8 feet) long, this was based on juvenile and sub-adult specimens, suggesting the adult may have been larger.
facts.quote: According to the 2017 article which officially named and described Moabosaurus, the animal was said to reach 10 meters (32.8 feet) long. However, the specimens which were examined belonged to juveniles and sub-adults, so it's possible that the creature measured longer when fully-grown.

facts.statement: A 2017 analysis classified Moabosaurus as a basal titanosauriform macronarian neosauropod.
facts.quote: Phylogenetic analyses in the describing article in 2017 indicated that Moabosaurus is a basal titanosauriform macronarian neosauropod.

facts.statement: A second 2017 study placed Moabosaurus in the Turiasauria, outside of the Neosauropoda.
facts.quote: However, a second study which was made in 2017 placed it in the Turiasauria, thus outside of the Neosauropoda.

facts.statement: Moabosaurus shares derived features with Turiasaurus, including a specific braincase structure, bifurcated cervical ribs, low neural spines, and strongly procoelous proximal caudal vertebrae.
facts.quote: With Turiasaurus it shares derived features of the braincase; bifurcated cervical (neck) ribs; extremely low neural spines on the cervical and anterior dorsal vertebrae; and strongly procoelous proximal caudal vertebrae.

facts.statement: Unlike other titanosauriform sauropods, Moabosaurus had thick-walled vertebrae with large pneumatic chambers and large, spatulate teeth similar to Camarasaurus.
facts.quote: Unlike other titanosauriform sauropods it has thick-walled vertebrae with large pneumatic chambers (camerate-grade) as in basal macronarians and large, spatulate teeth, as in Camarasaurus.

facts.statement: Moabosaurus utahensis is the only known species of extinct Moabosaurus, a titanosauriform sauropod that lived approximately 125 million years ago during the Barremian in what is now North America.
facts.quote: Moabosaurus utahensis es la única especie conocida del género extinto Moabosaurus ("lagarto de Moab") de dinosaurio saurópodo titanosauriforme que vivió a principios del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 125 millones de años durante el Barremiense en lo que es hoy Norteamérica.

facts.statement: The Paleobiology Database records the time range for Moabosaurus as the Valanginian, from 137.05 to 132.6 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Valanginian to Valanginian (137.05 to 132.6 million years ago)

facts.statement: The Dalton Wells quarry has yielded fossils of coexisting dinosaurs including the brachiosaurid Venenosaurus, theropods Utahraptor and Nedcolbertia, a tall-spined iguanodontian, and the ankylosaurian Gastonia.
facts.quote: The Dalton Wells quarry has also yielded specimens of Venenosaurus (a brachiosaurid sauropod), the theropod dinosaurs Utahraptor and Nedcolbertia, plus a tall-spined iguanodontian, and the ankylosaurian Gastonia.

facts.statement: Non-dinosaurian taxa at the Dalton Wells quarry are rare and limited to fragments of a pterosaur, crocodilians, turtles, and a neochoristodere.
facts.quote: Los taxones no dinosaurios son raros en la cantera y se limitan a fragmentos de un pterosaurio, crocodilianos, tortugas, y un neocoristodero.
